big: Most Indian portfolios hold only Indian assets. An international fund adds a second thing that can move your money: the rupee. This lesson shows how both work, and where the door is sometimes closed.

lines: A friend put 20% of his money in a US fund and says the rupee fall made him extra profit. Should I copy him?
The rupee can help, or it can hurt. Let us put ₹1 lakh through three different rupee years and see.

alt: Four bars: 1 lakh rupees invested, and its value after the fund gains 5 percent in dollars under three rupee scenarios
caps: ₹1 lakh buys $1,250 when a dollar costs ₹80. The foreign fund gains 5% in dollars: $1,312.50.
Rupee steady at ₹80: that is ₹1,05,000, up 5%.
Rupee weakens to ₹86: the same dollars are worth ₹1,12,875, up about 12.9%.
Rupee strengthens to ₹76: the dollars are worth ₹99,750, a loss of 0.25% despite a 5% gain.

h: A slice abroad, ten made-up years
alt: Three lines: India alone, a global fund in rupees, and an 80 20 blend
caps: Made-up decade, not real data. Assume the rupee weakens about 3% a year. It can also strengthen.
India falls in years 2 and 4. The global fund, in rupee terms, rises in both.
Another year, the global fund falls and India holds up. They do not move in step.
The 80% India, 20% global blend had a deepest fall of about 9%, against 15% for India alone.

q: A client invests ₹1 lakh in a foreign fund when ₹80 buys a dollar. The fund gains 5% in dollars and the rupee falls to ₹86 a dollar. What is the investment worth in rupees?
opts: About ₹1,05,000, since the 5% gain in dollars is the only gain that counts
About ₹1,12,500, since the 5% and the 7.5% fall in the rupee add up directly
About ₹1,07,500, since only the rupee's fall counts when the fund holds dollars
About ₹1,12,875: dollars rose 5% and each dollar now fetches more rupees
why: That figure holds the rupee at ₹80. In this case it moved to ₹86, which adds to the rupee value.
The two effects multiply: 1.05 times 86 over 80. Adding them gives ₹1,12,500, slightly too low.
The fund also gained 5% in dollars. Counting only the currency move ignores half of the story.
₹1 lakh buys $1,250, which grows to $1,312.50. At ₹86 that is ₹1,12,875, about 12.9% more.

q: The same fund gains 5% in dollars, but the rupee strengthens from ₹80 to ₹76 a dollar. What does the investor see in rupees?
opts: About a 0.25% loss, since the stronger rupee cancels the gain in dollars
A 5% gain, since the foreign asset's return is not affected by the rupee
A 10% gain, since a stronger rupee adds to the 5% earned in dollars
A 5% loss, since a stronger rupee wipes out the dollar gain and more besides
why: 1.05 times 76 divided by 80 is 0.9975, about a 0.25% fall. Currency can erase a foreign gain.
The rupee value of a foreign holding does depend on the exchange rate. A 5% dollar gain is not 5% in rupees.
A stronger rupee means each dollar buys fewer rupees. It reduces the rupee value, not adds to it.
The dollar fell about 5% against the rupee, which offsets the 5% gain. The net loss is only about 0.25%.

q: A client wants 20% in a US fund because the rupee always weakens. How should the adviser respond?
opts: Agree, since the rupee has weakened in every year and will do so in every future year
Agree, as a weak rupee makes any foreign fund a sure win for an Indian investor
A weaker rupee can add to returns, but it may reverse; the real case is spreading risk
Disagree, because a global fund holds no foreign currency at all, so the rupee does not matter
why: The rupee does not weaken every year. A strong year can cut the rupee value of foreign holdings.
A weak rupee helps, but a falling foreign market can still produce a loss. Nothing is a sure win.
The currency effect is real but runs both ways. The sounder reasons are geographic and currency diversification.
The rupee value of a foreign fund depends on the exchange rate, so the currency does matter.

q: An adviser plans to invest a ₹5 lakh lump sum into an international fund of funds next week. What should he do first?
opts: Check nothing, since overseas limits apply only to redemptions and never to purchases
Check whether the scheme is taking fresh money, as overseas limits can pause buying
Wait for the rupee to weaken before buying, since that is the right moment to buy
Switch the plan to an Indian equity fund, since overseas funds can never be bought
why: The limits restrict fresh subscriptions. Redemptions of units already held are a separate matter.
SEBI's industry-wide overseas limits can restrict fresh inflows, so availability and the cap on lump sums come first.
Timing the rupee is a guess. It is not a condition for buying, and the rupee can move either way.
Overseas funds can be bought. They just need a check on whether the scheme is open for fresh money.

pts: An international fund adds geographic and currency diversification. A weaker rupee raises rupee returns; a stronger one lowers them.
₹1 lakh at ₹80 per dollar, up 5% in dollars: ₹1,12,875 at ₹86, ₹99,750 at ₹76. The currency decides the rest.
SEBI's overseas limits can pause fresh inflows. Check availability before you plan a purchase.
